label: Scene Planes and Homographies
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 325 through 343 and turns a scene plane into a direct image-to-image transfer rule. A world plane seen by two cameras induces a single projective homography between the two images, replacing point-by-point triangulation with one transfer matrix that we will dissect, test, and connect to the fundamental matrix.

label: A Plane Induces a Homography
notes: Trace a ray through an image point until it meets the chosen plane, project that intersection into the second view, and the composition is a projective map. Because the plane is fixed, the same three by three matrix sends every planar point from one image to the other, giving the plane-induced homography H.

label: The Calibrated Formula
notes: For calibrated cameras with second camera rotation R and translation t, a plane with unit normal n at depth d induces H equal to K-prime times R minus t n transpose over d, all times K inverse. The rank-one term encodes translation scaled by inverse depth; rotation supplies the rest of the warp.

label: Homography From a Plane, Plane From H
notes: The map runs both directions. Given the plane and motion we read off H by the formula; given H and the camera pair we factor it back into a rotation part and a rank-one translation part, recovering the plane normal and depth up to the usual ambiguities. Decomposition generically yields two physically plausible solutions.

label: Compatibility With F
notes: A plane homography and the fundamental matrix are not independent. Any valid plane homography satisfies F equal to the skew of the second epipole times H, and equivalently H transpose F plus F transpose H equals zero. This is the algebraic statement that the transferred point Hx lies on the epipolar line of x.

label: Plane Plus Parallax
notes: Apply H to an off-plane point and you predict the image of where its ray pierces the plane, not the true correspondence. The residual from Hx to the real x-prime is parallax: it points along the epipolar line toward the epipole, and its length grows with the point's relative depth off the plane.

label: Parallax Scales With Relative Depth
notes: The parallax magnitude is governed by the ratio of the point's distance off the plane to its depth, multiplied by the camera baseline. Points on the plane have zero parallax; the further a point sits from the plane, the longer its displacement from Hx along the epipolar line toward the epipole.

label: Recovering F From a Plane Homography
notes: Plane plus parallax inverts into an estimation recipe. With a plane homography and the parallax of a few off-plane points, the epipole sits at the common intersection of the parallax join lines, and F equals the skew of that epipole times H. Two off-plane points generically pin the epipole down.

label: The Infinite Homography
notes: Let the plane recede to infinity, or equivalently drop the translation term, and H reduces to K-prime R K inverse, the infinite homography. It transfers vanishing points and directions between the views, isolates the rotation-only part of the motion, and is the backbone of camera calibration and rotation estimation.

label: Homologies and Plane Transfer
notes: When a plane homography fixes a point and a line of points, it is a planar homology, the structure behind symmetry and shadow relations between two coplanar configurations in one image. The infinite homography composes successive transfers, letting a known plane relay correspondences across a whole image sequence.

label: Applications
notes: Two staples follow directly. Image mosaicing stitches pure-rotation or planar-scene frames by chaining homographies into one panorama. Metric rectification removes projective and affine distortion from an imaged plane using the imaged circular points, recovering true angles and length ratios on facades, floors, and calibration targets.

label: Takeaways
notes: A nondegenerate world plane induces a full-rank image homography H equal to K-prime times R minus t n transpose over d times K inverse. It is compatible with F, off-plane points reveal themselves through epipolar parallax, and the infinite homography isolates rotation. Together these power transfer, rectification, and mosaicing.
